distillation_scope.scope_note: A bloodstream infection syndrome caused by Enterobacterales with an ESBL phenotype. Species, source, shock state, healthcare exposure, host immune status, and carbapenem resistance are represented as axes, risk factors, treatment modifiers, or future related leaves rather than as disease-name qualifiers.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Density and persistence of viable ESBL-producing Enterobacterales in the bloodstream after seeding from urinary, biliary, intra-abdominal, catheter, pulmonary, or occult sources.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: ESBL beta-lactam hydrolysis and resistance phenotype
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Plasmid-mediated or chromosomal ESBL activity that hydrolyzes extended-spectrum cephalosporins and aztreonam, often co-traveling with fluoroquinolone, aminoglycoside, or TMP-SMX resistance determinants.
Release of Enterobacterales from a tissue reservoir or device into blood; activity is sustained by obstruction, abscess, infected catheter, infected endovascular material, or inadequate drainage.
LPS and other PAMP-triggered TLR/complement activation producing fever, rigors, tachycardia, tachypnea, neutrophil mobilization, and endothelial activation.
Hepatic acute-phase reprogramming that raises CRP, procalcitonin, fibrinogen early, ferritin variably, and lowers albumin during systemic inflammation.
Sepsis-associated vasodilation, capillary leak, myocardial depression, and microcirculatory dysfunction producing hypotension, lactate elevation, oxygenation impairment, and shock progression.
Endothelial tissue-factor activation, platelet consumption, fibrinolysis dysregulation, and microvascular thrombosis that may evolve into overt DIC.
Kidney, liver, brain, lung, and metabolic injury from hypoperfusion, inflammatory endothelial injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, and delayed active therapy.

Ongoing positive blood cultures and hematogenous seeding of endovascular material, valves, vertebrae, kidney, liver, or soft-tissue abscesses, especially when source control or active therapy is delayed.
Reduced bacterial clearance or blunted inflammatory display from neutropenia, transplant immunosuppression, ESRD/hemodialysis, diabetes, advanced age, cirrhosis, or critical illness.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: A tissue or device nidus seeds Enterobacterales into blood.
ESBL enzymes make many empiric cephalosporin or aztreonam regimens inactive.
Ceftriaxone non-susceptibility is a core phenotypic consequence of ESBL production.
Cefepime MIC may appear low in some isolates but ESBL phenotype creates inoculum and failure risk in serious bacteremia.
Confirmed ESBL phenotype is the microbiology evidence that distinguishes this resistance leaf from ordinary Enterobacterales bacteremia.
Prior colonization, recent antibiotics, and healthcare exposure raise the posterior probability that the bloodstream isolate is ESBL-producing.
Resistance often manifests clinically as persistent fever or bacteremia under inactive empiric therapy.
Delayed active therapy prolongs inflammatory and ischemic injury.
Higher viable bloodstream burden increases the probability that blood cultures are positive.
Enterobacterales bacteremia is gram-negative bacteremia.
High bloodstream burden shortens time to positivity and increases quantitative culture signal when measured.
Inadequate therapy or uncontrolled focus extends the duration of positive cultures.
Urinary tract is the most common source of ESBL Enterobacterales bacteremia.
Biliary obstruction or cholangitis can seed ESBL Enterobacterales into blood.
Intra-abdominal infection and abscess are important sources and high-inoculum contexts.
Vascular or urinary devices can serve as an ESBL Enterobacterales source.
Obstruction, abscess, infected line, or infected prosthetic material require drainage, decompression, or removal.
Before drainage or line removal, the source remains uncontrolled.
Fever is common but may be absent in older or immunosuppressed hosts.
Cytokine release raises measured temperature.
Bacteremia frequently presents with chills or rigors from pyrogenic cytokines.
Fever, catecholamines, and sepsis physiology produce tachycardia.
Sepsis, fever, and metabolic acidosis raise respiratory rate.
Myeloid demargination and marrow release commonly produce leukocytosis; severe or immunosuppressed cases may be leukopenic.
Bacterial bloodstream infection usually drives neutrophilia unless marrow response is impaired.
Severe bacterial infection can produce a left shift.
IL-6 acute-phase signaling drives CRP elevation.
Bacterial sepsis often raises procalcitonin, particularly in bloodstream infection and shock.
Inflammation, capillary leak, and illness reduce serum albumin.
Distributive vasodilation lowers MAP.
Shock physiology can lower systolic pressure.
Hypoperfusion and impaired oxygen extraction raise lactate.
High vasodilatory shock activity is the event hazard for shock progression.
Septic AKI and urinary obstruction raise creatinine.
AKI, dehydration, and catabolism raise BUN.
Shock or obstructive urinary source may reduce urine output.
Septic encephalopathy and uremia can produce confusion or somnolence.
Renal hypoperfusion and inflammatory tubular injury raise AKI hazard.
Sepsis-induced platelet consumption lowers platelet count.
Consumptive coagulopathy prolongs PT/INR.
Fibrin formation and breakdown raise D-dimer.
Coagulopathy activity is the mechanistic bridge to overt DIC.
Failure to clear cultures reflects persistent bloodstream infection.
Persistent bacteremia can seed deep abscesses, vertebrae, or other metastatic foci.
Endocarditis is uncommon but important with prosthetic valves, persistent bacteremia, or hemodialysis access.
Impaired host clearance allows higher or longer bloodstream burden.
Neutropenia, marrow suppression, or immunosuppression can blunt leukocytosis.
Older adults and immunosuppressed hosts may have low or absent fever despite bacteremia.
Organ dysfunction is the dominant near-term driver of death.
Septic shock sharply raises early mortality.
Persistent bacteremia and metastatic complications prolong hazard after the initial sepsis window.
Severe systemic infection, shock, hypoxemia, ARDS, pulmonary edema, or fluid overload can increase oxygen or ventilatory support needs; this parallels the existing respiratory_rate pathway.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Fever and tachycardia co-move through cytokine and sympathetic tone.
Rising lactate and falling MAP jointly express septic shock physiology.
Active therapy rapidly reduces viable bacteremia when source control is adequate.
Delay to active therapy worsens survival in severe ESBL bacteremia.
Falling platelets are part of sepsis-induced coagulopathy and DIC risk.
High D-dimer reflects fibrin turnover and DIC physiology.
Rising creatinine marks and predicts AKI event state.
Biliary obstruction sustains bacteremia until drainage.
Persistent bacteremia increases concern for endovascular infection.
Ongoing bacteremia can seed deep foci.
Both acute-phase markers co-vary but are driven by upstream mechanisms rather than each other.
Shock transition sharply raises near-term mortality hazard.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Microbiologic activity is required for pathogen killing.
Carbapenemase or combined porin/efflux mechanisms reduce carbapenem effect.
High-inoculum abscess, obstruction, catheter, or device source cannot be reliably sterilized by antibiotics alone.
Severe beta-lactam reaction history may preclude carbapenem use or require specialist-supervised administration.
Dose adjustment is needed to avoid neurotoxicity while preserving exposure.

side_effects.interpretation: Rare neurotoxicity, higher with renal impairment or CNS disease.
Selection pressure and C. difficile risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Broad carbapenem option when ESBL bacteremia is severe, source is uncertain, Pseudomonas co-coverage is needed, or ertapenem exposure may be inadequate.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Ertapenem requires carbapenem-susceptible Enterobacterales.
Ertapenem lacks Pseudomonas activity if the syndrome may not be limited to Enterobacterales.
CRE risk reduces expected carbapenem activity.
High-inoculum source still needs drainage or removal.
Renal dosing is required.

treatments.context_specific_role: Narrower once-daily carbapenem option for susceptible ESBL Enterobacterales bacteremia when non-fermenter coverage is not needed and exposure is reliable.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Pathogen must be carbapenem susceptible.
CRE mechanisms reduce imipenem activity.
Renal impairment increases neurotoxicity risk.

side_effects.interpretation: Higher seizure signal than meropenem in susceptible hosts.

treatments.context_specific_role: Carbapenem alternative when local dosing, susceptibility, and toxicity context support use.

High-inoculum source worsens beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor reliability.

side_effects.interpretation: AKI signal, especially with concurrent vancomycin or shock.

treatments.context_specific_role: Potential empiric or de-escalation candidate only when susceptibility, severity, inoculum, and source-control context make effective coverage plausible.

supportive_care.clinical_role: Defines culture clearance and severity trajectory without using species identity as a diagnosis label.
Supports perfusion while antibiotics and source control reshape the disease trajectory.

quality_notes: Species, source, shock state, healthcare association, and host immunosuppression are not disease-name qualifiers.
Ceftriaxone/cefepime/piperacillin-tazobactam/carbapenem susceptibility are treatment modifiers, not diagnosis labels.
Carbapenemase risk is represented as a boundary modifier; a CRE-specific disease leaf may be needed for high-carbapenem-resistance cases.
